newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Iscor says interest in Zaire long term.
newsitem.headline: Iscor says interest in Zaire long term.

text.p: South African iron and steel company Iscor Ltd said on Wednesday Zaire's political and economic situation could improve dramatically and that the company's present interest in Zaire was a long-term investment.

Iscor reached a co-operation agreement with Zaire's state mining company Gecamines in February, winning the right to complete a feasibility study for the rehabilitation of the Kamato copper/cobalt mine in Shaba province.

"We believe that the Zairean nation's current fluid political and economic status has great potential for improvement and for the fact that we view our relationships as a long term investment, Iscor is committed to developing its relationships and portfolio of projects within Zaire for the long term benefit of the company, foreign partners and the people of Zaire," Iscor said in a statement.
It said Iscor's mining division had been involved in Zaire for several years "as Zaire is exceptionally blessed with some of the largest and richest mineral deposits in the world".

"Mining projects generally come to fruition after several years and last for decades. As such we are focusing on the long term potential of the country, and not necessarily on its immediate situation," the statement said.
The ore reserves at Kamato are estimated to be 66 million tonnes at 4.4 percent copper and 0.5 percent cobalt.
Iscor said when the agreement was announced that its aim was to bring the mine to its previous production level of two million tonnes of ore a year as soon as possible.
It said the rehabilitation of the mine could begin as early as the fourth quarter of 1997.
Iscor is one of several international mining companies active or interested in Zaire.
Others include Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd, Gencor Ltd, Barrick Gold Corp, Tenke Mining Corp, America Mineral Fields Inc and Ashanti Goldfields Company Ltd.

Stockbrokers Investec Securities said on Wednesday that production and exploration in Zaire had continued near normal despite the advance of rebel leader Laurent Kabila's soldiers -- who now controlled about half of the country.

"Mining companies already operating in Zaire are watching events with much apprehension but should remain confident that a ratification of their existing positions can be concluded with the rebel leaders," Investec said.
